costGuide.title: Skoda CNHA Engine Replacement Cost (UK)
costGuide.labourLine: Fitting a Skoda CNHA typically takes 8-11 hours at £65-£85/hr (independent specialist) - the EA288's transverse inline-4 layout is straightforward to access, keeping labour costs moderate compared to V6 or longitudinal platforms .
paragraphs: The primary cost driver for a Skoda CNHA replacement is the condition of the AdBlue dosing system and the Diesel Particulate Filter. A quality reconditioned unit will have the AdBlue injector, NOx sensors, and DPF verified or replaced, preventing the immediate recurrence of the engine's most common emissions-related faults. failures.title: Skoda CNHA Engine Problems - What Actually Fails

items.title: AdBlue System & NOx Sensor Faults - 2015-2020 models
items.whatHappens: The Selective Catalytic Reduction (SCR) system on the CNHA is prone to dosing pump failures, crystallised AdBlue deposits in the injector nozzle, and faulty NOx sensors. This triggers dashboard warning lights and, if left unresolved, initiates a countdown to a no-start condition mandated by Euro 6 legislation.
items.repairVsReplace: The dosing pump, injector, or sensors can typically be replaced independently at moderate cost. However, if AdBlue fluid has leaked into the DPF or if prolonged fault neglect has caused the SCR catalyst to degrade, a full Skoda CNHA replacement may prove more economical than stacking individual repairs. Read our full DPF failure guide .

items.title: DPF Clogging (Urban Use)
items.whatHappens: Frequent short, low-speed journeys prevent the Diesel Particulate Filter from reaching the temperatures required for active regeneration. Progressive soot accumulation restricts exhaust flow, triggering limp mode, loss of power, and eventually a blocked filter that cannot regenerate even on a motorway run.
items.repairVsReplace: Forced regenerations or chemical cleans can resolve mild clogging. A heavily ash-loaded DPF requires physical replacement. If the blockage has caused excessive exhaust backpressure and damaged the turbocharger turbine, a full Skoda CNHA replacement becomes the most reliable solution.

items.title: EGR Cooler Leaks
items.whatHappens: The Exhaust Gas Recirculation cooler can develop internal cracks over time, allowing coolant to seep into the exhaust gas stream or the intake manifold. Symptoms include unexplained coolant loss with no visible external leak, white exhaust smoke on warm-up, and rough running.
items.repairVsReplace: The EGR cooler is a bolt-on replacement and does not require engine removal. However, if coolant ingestion has been severe enough to cause hydraulic lock and bent connecting rods, a full Skoda CNHA replacement is mandatory.

failures.goodYearsLine: The CNHA benefits from the Gen 3 EA288 architecture, which is significantly more reliable than the preceding EA189 generation - the timing chain is robust, the injectors are durable, and the bottom end is well-proven. The dominant issues are emissions-system related rather than mechanical, and post-2017 units received minor AdBlue system revisions that reduced crystallisation complaints .

variants.title: How to Confirm You Have the Skoda CNHA
variants.intro: The Skoda CNHA engine code is stamped on a machined pad on the engine block, typically visible near the oil filter housing or on the cylinder head flange. It is also recorded on the vehicle's VIN plate under the bonnet and can be decoded from the VIN itself via a reliable online checker or your V5C registration document.

buyingGuide.title: Buying a Replacement Skoda CNHA - What to Choose

options.label: Used
options.body: A used Skoda CNHA is viable if it comes with a full service history confirming regular oil changes and, critically, documented AdBlue system top-ups and DPF regeneration cycles. The EA288 is mechanically robust, so a low-mileage used unit from a motorway-driven Octavia or Superb is often a sound investment - but verify the emissions system health before committing.

options.label: Reconditioned
options.body: A proper reconditioned Skoda CNHA is the recommended choice for most owners. A reputable specialist will verify or replace the AdBlue dosing module, NOx sensors, DPF, and EGR cooler, and will replace all critical seals and the timing belt. This effectively resets the engine's reliability clock while retaining the correct 150hp TDI Ultra calibration.

options.label: Rebuilt
options.body: A full rebuild is justified if the block or cylinder head has suffered damage - for example, from hydraulic lock caused by an EGR cooler leak, or from a seized turbo sending debris into the intake. Ensure the rebuilder uses updated emissions components and verifies the block's straightness before reassembly.

buyingGuide.supplyFitLine: Opting for a supply-and-fit service through our network ensures the replacing garage assumes full responsibility for both the unit and the labour, backed by a minimum 12-month warranty for complete peace of mind.
buyingGuide.vehicleValueNote: The Skoda CNHA was fitted to Octavia III and Superb III models, which typically hold retained values between £5,000 and £18,000 depending on age, mileage, and specification . The EA288 2.0 TDI carries a Safe replacement-to-value flag: reconditioned supply costs of £2,800-£4,500 remain well within the vehicle's retained value on most examples, making a professional engine replacement a financially sound decision rather than a write-off scenario.

items.question: How much does a Skoda CNHA engine replacement cost?
items.answer: A reconditioned Skoda CNHA engine typically costs between £2,800 and £4,500 for supply-only, with fully fitted prices ranging from £3,320 to £5,215. Pricing is estimated using the VW/Audi EA288 2.0 TDI as a baseline proxy, as the CNHA is the Skoda-specific designation of the same physical engine. Labour typically takes 8-11 hours due to standard transverse inline-4 packaging and ancillary removal requirements. Used units start around £1,200 but carry significant risk of inheriting AdBlue or DPF faults.

items.question: What is the most common Skoda CNHA engine failure?
items.answer: The dominant failures are AdBlue system faults (NOx sensors, dosing pump) and DPF clogging from urban use, typically manifesting between 80,000 and 180,000 miles. The Selective Catalytic Reduction system is prone to dosing pump failures or crystallised AdBlue in the injector, triggering warning lights and eventual no-start countdowns. Frequent short, low-speed journeys prevent the DPF from reaching regeneration temperatures, leading to progressive soot accumulation and limp mode. EGR cooler leaks are also reported at higher mileages, which can cause unexplained coolant loss or, in severe cases, hydrolock damage.

items.question: Which Skoda models use the CNHA engine?
items.answer: The Skoda CNHA was widely fitted as the efficient, high-torque 150hp diesel option across the brand's core lineup, specifically powering the Octavia Mk3 (5E) and Superb Mk3 (3V) 2.0 TDI 150 badges. Production spanned from 2013 (Octavia) and 2015 (Superb) through 2020, serving as the primary diesel powerplant for the 150hp model designation. It was never fitted to entry-level 1.6 TDI models or higher-output 184hp SportLine variants, which use different engine codes.

items.question: Should I buy a used or reconditioned Skoda CNHA engine?
items.answer: A properly reconditioned Skoda CNHA is strongly recommended over a used unit for this specific engine. A quality reconditioned unit will have the AdBlue dosing module, NOx sensors, and DPF verified or replaced, preventing the immediate recurrence of the engine's most common faults. Used units are a gamble; without documented proof of emissions system maintenance, you risk inheriting imminent AdBlue or DPF failures that can trigger no-start conditions. The cost difference is justified by the comprehensive 12-24 month warranty that accompanies a reconditioned unit.

items.question: How do I confirm my car has the CNHA engine code?
items.answer: You can verify the CNHA engine code by checking the VIN plate under the bonnet, your V5C registration document, or the physical stamp on the engine block. The code is typically stamped on a machined pad near the oil filter housing or on the cylinder head. Do not confuse it with the CRKB (115hp), CUNA (184hp), or CRLB (150hp pre-Ultra calibration); the "CNHA" designation is critical, as it denotes the specific 150hp TDI Ultra efficiency tune. If you are unsure, our registration lookup tool will confirm your exact engine code before any quotes are generated.
